scenes.text: A 70 billion parameter model needs about 140 gigabytes of memory. [1] That's way more than any gaming GPU. [2] Yet people run it at home. The trick is quantization. Let's see how it works.

[1] Quantization means storing the model's numbers with less precision. [2] Normally, each weight uses 16 bits. [3] Quantization rounds them to 8 bits, or even 4 bits. [4] The model gets much smaller, and faster, with only a small loss in quality.

data.definition: Storing a model's weights with fewer bits, like 8 or 4 instead of 16, to make it smaller and faster.

scenes.text: Think of a photo. [1] The original is a huge, high resolution file. [2] A compressed version is a fraction of the size, and on your phone screen, it looks almost the same. Quantization does this, for AI weights.

right.title: Compressed
right.label: tiny file, looks almost the same

scenes.text: [1] Here's the math for a 70 billion parameter model. [2] At 16 bits, about 140 gigabytes. [3] At 8 bits, about 70 gigabytes. [4] And at 4 bits, about 35 gigabytes. That's a quarter of the size.

So how does it work? [1] Look at a group of weights, and find their range. [2] Divide that range into a few steps, like 16 steps for 4 bits. [3] Round each weight to the nearest step, and store just the step number, plus one scale value.

data.heading: How it works
steps: Each weight to its nearest step

scenes.text: Here are four terms. [1] Precision, how many bits each number uses. [2] GGUF, a popular file format for quantized models you run at home. [3] Q4, shorthand for a 4 bit version. [4] And perplexity, a score that shows how much quality was lost.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think quantized models are broken, low quality copies. [2] At 8 bits, most people can't tell the difference. At 4 bits, there's a small drop. Only very low bits, like 2 bits, hurt a lot.

data.myth: Quantized models are broken, low quality copies.
data.fact: 8-bit is nearly identical, 4-bit drops a little. Only very low bits, like 2-bit, hurt a lot.

scenes.text: Quick quiz! A model is 140 gigabytes at 16 bits. About how big is it at 4 bits? [1] Pause and think, and if you get it right, comment below! <pause 3.2> [2] About 35 gigabytes, a quarter of the size!

Let's recap. [1] Quantization stores weights with fewer bits. [2] 16 bits to 8, or 4. [3] Models get much smaller and faster. [4] And 4 bits is often the sweet spot for quality. [5] Next, how to run AI models on your own laptop. Follow AI Maastaaru!
